extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers preparing research reports and data visualizations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing research-report introductions, conclusions, and for designing tables, charts, and graphs that communicate evidence clearly and ethically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shade rows in large tables
rubrics_metrics.description: For tables with many rows, lightly shade every fifth row.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Light shading helps readers track rows across wide tables. Keep shading subtle so it doesn't overwhelm the data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use grid lines sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Use background grid lines only if the graphic is complex or readers need to see precise numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make grid lines light gray so they aid reading without dominating the image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use color only when useful and reproducible
rubrics_metrics.description: Color or shade lines or bars only to show a contrast. Use color only if the text will be printed in color and not photocopied later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Black-and-white photocopies can make many colors look alike; if print/photocopy reproduction is uncertain, rely on distinct patterns or grayscale contrasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid iconic bars and gratuitous 3-D
rubrics_metrics.description: Never use iconic bars (for example, images of cars to represent automobile production) or add a third dimension merely for effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both iconic bars and unnecessary 3-D look amateurish and can distort how readers judge values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use three-dimensional plots only when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot data on three dimensions only when your readers are familiar with such graphs and you cannot display the data in any other way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 3-D can obscure values and relationships; prefer 2-D representations unless 3-D is required and understandable by the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label all table rows, columns, and axes
rubrics_metrics.description: Label all rows and columns in tables and both axes in charts and graphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear labels prevent reader confusion. Use descriptive labels rather than shorthand where space allows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tick marks and interval labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tick marks and labels to indicate intervals on the vertical axis of a graph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tick marks make it easier to read approximate values; choose interval spacing appropriate to the data range and audience needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer inline labels to separate legends
rubrics_metrics.description: If possible, label lines, bar segments, and the like on the image rather than in a legend set to the side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a legend only if inline labels would make the image too complex to read. Inline labels reduce eye movement between figure and legend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show exact numbers when they matter
rubrics_metrics.description: When specific numbers matter, add them to bars or segments in charts or to dots on lines in graphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotating exact values helps readers who need precise information; for dense graphics, choose the most important data points to label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order table rows/columns by useful principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Order the rows and columns by a principle that lets readers quickly find what you want them to see; do not automatically choose alphabetic order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize to highlight patterns or comparisons (e.g., by size, by groupings). Use an informative title and reduce visual clutter to reveal the pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round numbers to relevant precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Round numbers to a relevant value; avoid irrelevant precision (e.g., don't show 2,123,499 if differences under 1,000 don't matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excess precision distracts and implies false accuracy. Choose rounding consistent with the meaningful resolution of the data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place totals at logical ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Sum totals at the bottom of a column or at the end of a row, not at the top or left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers expect totals at bottoms/end positions; placing them elsewhere reduces readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange bars to support the message
rubrics_metrics.description: Group and arrange bars to create an image that matches your message; avoid arbitrary (e.g., alphabetical) ordering that hides the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order bars to emphasize the pattern you want readers to see (e.g., regional clustering). Example: grouping deserts by region supports a claim about concentration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stacked bars when comparing whole values
rubrics_metrics.description: Use stacked bars only when you want readers to compare whole values for different bars rather than their divided segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers can't easily compare proportions of stacked segments by eye; use stacked bars to emphasize total heights, not fine-grained segment comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order stacked segments logically
rubrics_metrics.description: If you use stacked bars, arrange segments in a logical order; if possible put the largest segment at the bottom in the darkest shade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent ordering and shading help comparisons across bars; consider placing most important or stable segments at the bottom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label stacked segments and connect corresponding segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Label segments with specific numbers and, to assist comparisons, connect corresponding segments with gray lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numeric labels and connector lines reduce the difficulty of comparing segments across stacked bars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange grouped bars logically and consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: If you group bars because segments are as important as the wholes, arrange groups in a logical order and, if possible, put bars of similar size next to one another. Order bars the same way through all groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent internal ordering across groups helps readers compare like-with-like; consider visual balance and sequence of categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label groups with total values
rubrics_metrics.description: Label groups with the number for the whole, either above each group or below the labels on the bottom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing the total for each grouped cluster helps readers interpret both the whole and its parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pie charts for precise comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Pie charts are harder to read than bar charts and invite misinterpretation; most researchers consider them amateurish—use bar charts instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pie charts can be acceptable when showing one variable with very few, very different segments, but add numeric labels if used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose variable orientation to support your rhetorical point
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the variable that makes the line go in the direction (up or down) that supports your point (e.g., show retention as rising rather than dropouts as falling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing the plotted variable can make your point clearer; do not distort meaning—choose an equivalent variable representation that honestly expresses the data trend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit number of lines on a single graph
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot more than six lines on one graph only if you cannot make your point in any other way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too many lines create clutter and confusion; consider multiple panels or smaller multiples to separate series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark data points when data are sparse
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have fewer than ten or so data points, indicate them with dots; if only a few are relevant, insert numbers to show their exact value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dots and numeric labels help readers see individual observations in sparse series and reduce misreading of trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on shades of gray to distinguish lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not depend on different shades of gray to distinguish lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shades may not be distinct enough, causing flicking between legend and lines; use distinct markers, colors (when reproducible), or inline labels instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test alternative graphics and pretest with naive readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct alternative graphics; then ask someone unfamiliar with the data to judge them for impact and clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparing alternatives and getting outsider feedback helps choose the clearest representation. Always introduce figures with a sentence stating the claim you want the figure to support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid manipulating scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not manipulate a scale to magnify or reduce a contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truncated axes (e.g., starting y-axis at 80 instead of 0) exaggerate small contrasts; use scales that honestly represent the magnitude of changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid figures that distort values
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a figure whose image distorts values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: using dual axes with different scales to imply correlation, stacked-area placement that makes some bands seem to rise when they do not. Choose forms that show true relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary complexity or misleading simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make a table or figure unnecessarily complex or misleadingly simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex figures confuse readers; oversimplified figures can hide important variation. Balance clarity with completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the point the figure supports
rubrics_metrics.description: If the table or figure supports a point, state it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce figures with a sentence that explicitly states the claim they are meant to support so readers know how to interpret them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select graphic form to match rhetorical use
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the type of graphic (bar chart, grouped bars, stacked bars, histogram, map/diagram, pie chart, line graph, stacked area, scatterplot, bubble chart) according to what you want to show—comparisons across cases, segments within cases, distributions, trends, spatial patterns, proportions, relationships, or three-variable interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter's Table 15.7 maps common graphic forms to their best rhetorical uses and cautions (e.g., bar charts emphasize individual comparisons and ranks; grouped bars contrast subsets within cases; pie charts only for few segments; line graphs best for trends; scatterplots for distribution and outliers; bubble charts add a third variable but are easily misjudged—add numbers). Use the recommended form for the rhetorical purpose and annotate for specific values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use area charts cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Stacked area charts show totals plus contributions but can mislead readers about individual-case trends depending on stacking order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because area charts represent changes by area, bands placed on top of a rising band can falsely appear to rise; choose stacking order to avoid misleading impressions or use alternative forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce figures with a claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce the figures with a sentence that states the claim you want the figure to support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This orients readers to the intended interpretation before they examine the graphic; without it readers may miss the rhetorical point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction structure: Context + Problem + Response
rubrics_metrics.description: A full introduction typically consists of three elements: contextualizing background (common ground), a statement of the problem (disruption), and a response to the problem (your thesis or promise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not every introduction needs all three elements (omit common ground if problem is well known, omit consequences if obvious). Use the pattern to motivate readers and help them understand the paper's trajectory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish common ground for the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with a shared understanding that prepares readers to see why the problem matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide enough background to orient readers who know some of the field but not the specific issue; avoid skimping (which confuses non-specialists) and avoid over-surveying irrelevant sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the problem as condition plus consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: State the research problem by describing (1) a condition of incomplete knowledge or understanding, and (2) the consequences of that condition (the 'So what?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can state the condition directly or imply it as a question. Explain the consequences as a cost or a benefit to motivate readers; some audiences respond more to real costs than to potential benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide when to state the problem explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: State the condition of a problem explicitly when readers may not infer the gap; if the question is familiar, you may imply it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In natural and social sciences, readers often expect familiar questions; in humanities or novel inquiries, explicitly describe the knowledge gap so readers understand significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out consequences and benefits when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: To convince readers to care, state the tangible costs of not solving the problem or the benefits of solving it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied research often has tangible costs to highlight; pure research can describe misinterpretation or broader understanding as the consequence/benefit. If readers already know the consequences, you may omit them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test your problem statement with 'So what?'
rubrics_metrics.description: After stating the condition of ignorance or misunderstanding, ask 'So what?' to ensure the consequence is clear and persuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cannot answer 'So what?' succinctly, your problem statement may be unconvincing or too narrowly motivated; revise to show broader significance or find a different audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: State your response (thesis) or promise it
rubrics_metrics.description: Either state the gist of your solution toward the end of the introduction or promise the solution and launch the paper into a point-last structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stating the main point early helps readers; promising a solution can create suspense but must offer a clear conceptual outline or plan to guide the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague topic announcements
rubrics_metrics.description: The weakest openings merely announce a vague topic (e.g., 'This study investigates processes leading to ozone depletion').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide either a clear problem or a conceptual launching point; otherwise the introduction fails to motivate or orient readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set pace of introduction to audience knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide how quickly to raise the problem based on how much your readers already know; open quickly for peers, open slowly for less knowledgeable readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opening too quickly to novices will confuse them; opening too slowly to peers may suggest you know too little. Adjust 'speed' to match the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write conclusions using intro elements in reverse
rubrics_metrics.description: A conclusion should start with your main point, then restate significance or application; you can use the introduction's elements in reverse order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the main point near the beginning of the conclusion (more fully if already stated in the intro), then add new significance, application, or broader consequences (a new 'So what?').

rubrics_metrics.name: Start conclusion with the main point
rubrics_metrics.description: State your main point near the beginning of your conclusion; if stated earlier, repeat it more fully rather than verbatim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers expect a clear restatement of the thesis in the conclusion; expand it with additional insight rather than mere repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add new significance or application in conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: After your point, say why it's significant, preferably by adding a new answer to 'So what?' (e.g., policy, cultural, or disciplinary implications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid simply summarizing; provide a take-away that deepens or extends the reader's understanding of the consequences or next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be selective in surveying prior work
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey only those sources whose findings you will directly modify; avoid listing every source that remotely touches the topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overbroad literature surveys obscure your specific problem and can fatigue readers; include additional background only when necessary to locate the problem in a wider context.
